16                 THE SECRETARY:   Resolution 2285, by 

17    Senator Hinchey, mourning the death of 

18    Hudson Talbott, distinguished citizen, 

19    beloved writer, talented artist, and devoted 

20    member of his community.

21                 ACTING PRESIDENT PERSAUD:   Senator 

22    Hinchey on the resolution.

23                 SENATOR HINCHEY:   Madam President, 

24    I rise today to honor the life and unforgettable 

25    legacy of Mr. Hudson Talbott, a celebrated 


                                                                6751

 1    communicator, an international ambassador of 

 2    creativity, and a beloved resident of the 

 3    Hudson Valley.  

 4                 Hudson was a masterful writer, 

 5    illustrator and artist with a rare gift, the 

 6    ability to turn big ideas and thought-provoking 

 7    art into stories that resonate with people of all 

 8    ages.  He knew how to meet minds exactly where 

 9    their imaginations lived.  

10                 His work is celebrated worldwide, 

11    earning prestigious commissions from renowned 

12    institutions like the Louvre, in Paris, and 

13    closer to home at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, 

14    the Museum of Modern Art, and the Metropolitan 

15    Opera.  

16                 His calling was sparked unexpectedly 

17    when the Museum of Modern Art commissioned him to 

18    create a unique guide for young visitors titled 

19    "How to Show Grownups the Museum."  That project 

20    ignited a realization for Hudson.  It showed him 

21    that he could take the places and ideas most 

22    sacred to him, from the bustling energy of 

23    New York City to the quiet majesty of the 

24    Hudson River, and share that sense of wonder with 

25    children all over the world.  


                                                                6752

 1                 For over four decades, Hudson poured 

 2    his talents into awakening a sense of possibility 

 3    for his readers through his children's books.  He 

 4    turned prehistoric creatures into beloved 

 5    characters in We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story, and 

 6    collaborated with Steven Sondheim to adapt 

 7    Into the Woods for young readers.  

 8                 Perhaps most inspiring of all, 

 9    Hudson drew upon his own childhood struggles with 

10    dyslexia in his award-winning book A Walk in the 

11    Words.  It was his way of creating something to 

12    help children facing similar struggles who might 

13    find in its pages strength, understanding, and 

14    the realization that they are never alone.

15                 Beyond the bookshelves, Hudson was a 

16    devoted community leader.  He was a founding 

17    trustee of the Thomas Cole National Historic Site 

18    in Catskill, where he served for 20 years, 

19    sharing the richness of Thomas Cole's work and 

20    influence on American landscape painting.  

21                 Hudson inspired people to dream, to 

22    believe in themselves, and to remain infinitely 

23    curious.  What an incredible gift, that he could 

24    do this through the words that he brought to life 

25    in his books.


                                                                6753

 1                 The connections Hudson forged 

 2    between fine art, history, and children's 

 3    literature will be felt in the Hudson Valley and 

 4    around the world for generations to come.  

 5                 And on a personal note, Hudson was 

 6    an incredible friend.  You could feel his joy and 

 7    his love almost physically spill over when he 

 8    engaged in something that he loved or with 

 9    someone that he appreciated.  What a gift to have 

10    known Hudson and to have been a recipient of that 

11    warmth.  

12                 When I think about Catskill, I think 

13    of Hudson.  His love for the village, his 

14    excitement for the new businesses, his creation 

15    of the tight-knit community that exists today.  

16                 Hudson really is woven into the 

17    fabric of Catskill.  And I will think of him 

18    every time I have a cup of coffee at Willa's, or 

19    walk the main street, or celebrate Catskill Pride 

20    or look at the beautiful landscapes where we are 

21    so lucky to call home.

22                 Madam President, we are joined today 

23    by Hudson's incredible partner, Jay Lesenger, and 

24    his longtime assistant and close friend 

25    Amanda Collier.


                                                                6754

 1                 To you I extend my deep sympathies, 

 2    sincere sympathies.  Hudson will be truly missed.  

 3    He was larger than life, an incredible person, an 

 4    absolute joy, and someone who I feel so lucky and 

 5    privileged to have been able not just to know but 

 6    to call a friend.

 7                 Madam President, please offer our 

 8    guests all of the privileges and cordialities of 

 9    this chamber.

10                 Thank you very much.

17                 THE SECRETARY:   Resolution 1890, by 

18    Senator Hinchey, memorializing Governor Kathy 

19    Hochul to proclaim June 2026 as Dairy Month in 

20    the State of New York.

21                 ACTING PRESIDENT PERSAUD:   Senator 

22    Hinchey on the resolution.  

23                 ACTING PRESIDENT PERSAUD:   Thank 

24    you, Madam President.  

25                 Today here at the Capitol, it's one 


                                                                6758

 1    of my favorite days of the year, Dairy Day.  From 

 2    ice cream and yogurt to artisan cheeses and cold 

 3    glasses of milk, the dairy industry is New York's 

 4    leading ag specialty.  

 5                 This powerhouse sector thrives 

 6    thanks to a dedicated community of over 

 7    3,000 dairy farmers.  Unlike other parts of the 

 8    country, New York's dairy industry is not 

 9    dominated by corporate factory farms.  In our 

10    state, dairy was started, stewarded and expanded 

11    by generations of local families.  

12                 The invaluable wisdom passed down 

13    through these families is exactly why New York 

14    competes and leads on the national stage.  Today 

15    our state ranks proudly No. 1 in yogurt, 

16    sour cream and cottage cheese, and No. 4 in total 

17    dairy production.  

18                 Our farmers have done an incredible 

19    job in elevating New York dairy, and they're 

20    supported by strong collaborations with 

21    world-class research partners at Cornell CALS and 

22    local CCEs across the state.  Through that 

23    partnership, New York outproduces our neighbors 

24    in Pennsylvania and Vermont in total milk 

25    production.  


                                                                6759

 1                 New York dairy farmers are also 

 2    leading the way in sustainability, achieving a 

 3    42 percent decrease in greenhouse gas emissions 

 4    per gallon of milk, and a 24 percent reduction in 

 5    total farm emissions because of the practices 

 6    they've implemented to help steward our 

 7    environment.  

 8                 Their hard work has attracted over 

 9    $3.5 billion in new investment in New York over 

10    the next five years, making New York No. 1 in 

11    dairy manufacturing advancements across the 

12    country.  That's an incredible feat.  

13                 New York dairy punches well above 

14    its weight because of the grit, determination and 

15    love of our family farms.  We had a number of our 

16    local producers who were in the chamber with us 

17    earlier, and we had a great day at Dairy Day in 

18    the Well.  

19                 I want to give a special shout-out 

20    to Hudson Valley Fresh, who is an incredible 

21    co-op in my district who makes sure that all of 

22    our students are drinking good, healthy milk in 

23    our schools.  

24                 I rise to vote aye on this 

25    resolution and to support Dairy Month in the 


                                                                6760

 1    State of New York.

 2                  Thank you very much, 

 3    Madam President.

 4                 ACTING PRESIDENT PERSAUD:   Thank 

 5    you, Senator.

 6                 Senator Borrello on the resolution.

 7                 SENATOR BORRELLO:   Thank you, 

 8    Madam President.  

 9                 Well, if the two-story-tall 

10    inflatable cow didn't tell you that today was 

11    Dairy Day, you obviously missed something big.  

12                 You know, it is a great day to 

13    celebrate agriculture.  I want to thank our 

14    chairwoman of the Ag Committee, Senator Hinchey.  

15    I'm proud to be the ranking member of the 

16    Agriculture Committee.  

17                 And New York is an agriculture 

18    state, and it is a dairy state, that is for sure.  

19    As was mentioned, yogurt, cheese, so many great 

20    dairy products here in New York State that drive 

21    our economy, that make sure our food is made here 

22    locally to help our food security.  It is a huge 

23    economic engine that is so important.  

24                 It's tough to be a farmer here in 

25    New York State.  It's tough to be a farmer 


                                                                6761

 1    anywhere, quite frankly, but particularly here in 

 2    New York State.  But yet we are proud to have 

 3    nearly 98 percent of our farms are family-owned 

 4    farms.  

 5                 In my district there are over 

 6    4500 farms, literally one farm for every square 

 7    mile of the 57th Senate District, much of which 

 8    are dairy farms.  They are people that work hard 

 9    every day, they're proud of what they do.  They 

10    feed our families and they keep our people 

11    employed. 

12                 God bless those that farm.  And 

13    today we celebrate agriculture and dairy farms in 

14    particular.  Again, I'm proud to vote yes.  

15                 Thank you, Madam President.

17    Oberacker on the resolution.

19    Madam President.  

20                 As the proud pop-pop to two 

21    grandsons who are on their family dairy farm, 

22    Dairy Day, Dairy Month is every day on the farm 

23    for them.  

24                 Just the other day my grandson 

25    Daniel was explaining to me the proper way to 


                                                                6762

 1    chop hay.  And I was -- he's only four years old, 

 2    Madam President, and the job to educate the 

 3    Senator is not an easy one, as I'm sure most of 

 4    my colleagues in the chamber would agree to.  But 

 5    he did such a great job of explaining how that

 7    farmer-in-training than my grandson.

 9    work the farm in Columbia County.  God bless them 

10    for the life that they've chosen, the hard work 

11    that they put out every day.  

12                 Thank you to our chair for bringing 

13    this resolution forward.  And I, as a proud dairy 

14    pop-pop, proudly vote aye.  

15                 Thank you, Madam President.

 1    medical debt on their credit reports.  More than

 3    utility bills.  And over 2.4 million New Yorkers

 5    now our state's consumer protection laws protect

 7                 New York gives important consumer 

 8    protections when they're sued over credit card 

 9    debt, but those protections are confusing and 

10    outdated, and they don't reflect how the debt 

11    collection industry actually works.  In fact, 

12    they often don't apply to medical debt, 

13    rent arrears, tuition debt, utilities, and 

14    everyday consumer debts.  

15                 What does that mean for everyday 

16    New Yorkers?  The overwhelming majority of cases 

17    involve plaintiffs suing consumers without legal 

18    representation, without clear pleadings, notice, 

19    proper venue and fair deadlines, consumers often 

20    don't understand what they are being sued for or 

21    how to respond.  

22                 We all want a court system that 

23    treats New Yorkers with fairness and respect, but 

24    when it comes to these debt cases, that's not 

25    what we're getting.  The Consumer Debt Uniformity 


                                                                6823

 1    Act does a simple thing.  It extends existing 

 2    protections to all types of debt cases, including 

 3    requirements that the complaint provide basic 

 4    information about the alleged debt, along with 

 5    additional notices in multiple languages, clearer 

 6    notice on summary judgment motions, and more time 

 7    to raise improper service.  

 8                 In short, it brings our laws in line 

 9    with the times and ensures that New Yorkers 

10    aren't treated differently based on the type of 

11    debt being collected.  These protections help 

12    unrepresented consumers understand the cases 

13    against them and respond before losing by 

14    default.

15                 Believe it or not, this proposal is 

16    actually good for lenders too.  Clearer 

17    complaints and uniform rules make the process 

18    more predictable, improve consistency across 

19    courts, and help consumers identify and resolve 

20    valid debts more quickly.  

21                 It's about basic fairness,

24    debt, rent arrears, tuition debt and utility 

25    payments.  They face the same challenges and

 2    credit card debt, and they should be given the

13                 You know, as we often work in this 

14    chamber around a lot of key issues, none of us 

15    can most certainly deny the significance of 

16    improving access to public transportation.  And 

17    so this bill is aiming to do just that.  

18                 In districts like mine in the 

19    Southern Tier and upstate New York, having access 

20    to public transportation, especially in 

21    underserved areas, is very -- it's a challenge, 

22    but it also is something that we are aiming to 

23    address with this legislation.  

24                 In my district, access to a bus 

25    route is the difference between making it to a 


                                                                6876

 1    doctor's appointment or missing it, making it to 

 2    work or to school, making it to important 

 3    recreation opportunities with your family and 

 4    staying connected to our respective communities.

 5                 The Central New York Regional 

 6    Transportation Authority, also known as Centro, 

 7    is that lifeline for many residents in my 

 8    district.  Centro serves the counties of 

 9    Onondaga, Oswego, Cayuga, and Oneida.  And last 

10    year we passed legislation allowing Centro to 

11    expand their service area to include 

12    Cortland County, in my district, bringing 

13    reliable public transportation to a community 

14    that desperately needs it.

15                 Now that we have expanded the 

16    service, we must also expand representation.  And 

17    so Centro's board cannot effectively serve a 

18    community if it does not have a pathway to hear 

19    from constituents who have much needed input that 

20    will help guide their decisions.  

21                 And so what this bill will do is 

22    that it will allow Centro to increase their board 

23    from 12 to 13 members, creating the space for 

24    Cortland County to have a voice at the table.

25                 As we know, good governance isn't

 1    just about providing a service; we also have to

10    public transportation in the Southern Tier, and 

11    this bill is a step in the right direction.  

12                 I proudly vote aye.
